newsitem.title: UK: Bond markets may face last leg of rally.
newsitem.headline: Bond markets may face last leg of rally.

text.p: Bond markets are likely to stage a recovery from the shock given by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts said on Thursday.
However, that recovery could be the last move up, as investors may be faced with an imminent rise in U.S. interest rates, coupled with signs of strong growth in Europe.

"In the short term there is the prospect of a bounce back, as the impact of the testimony fades," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets. "But that will change in three to six months. I'd sell into strength."
On Wednesday, during his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Greenspan gave an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy but said he was concerned about inflation risks and the buoyant equity market.
He said the Fed may even raise interest rates before inflation picks up to ensure that economy stays on an even keel and that the nearly six-year-old expansion continues.
"We may decide to move ... before you see actual evidences of real inflation emerging," he said.
Dealers said Greenspan's impact on the debt markets, both in the U.S. and Europe, was swift and sure.
"Obviously the market was long at the time," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London.
"It was just panic selling. It was just carnage."
He said the market had stabilised for now but everything would depend on how New York looked at things following Wednesday's poor close. "The U.S. is going to lead."
The 30-year long bond lost 1-1/2 points on Wednesday to close at 98-03, yielding 6.77 percent.
T-notes significantly underperformed their German counterparts, with the 10-year T-note/Bund yield gap shooting seven basis points wider to over 100 basis points after Greenspan's speech.
By 0934 GMT on Thursday, the spread was at 106 basis points.

Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London, said markets were surprised by quite how hawkish Greenspan appeared, although he said it was still not a foregone conclusion that U.S. interest rates will rise.
"It's still a close call," he said.
Wattret at Paribas said he did not think the Fed would hike rates until May, once key data such as the first quarter GDP figures and the employment cost index have been released.
"We're going for a quarter-point rise in May, once we have seen the core rate of consumer price inflation rising," he said.
Chester, who was more sanguine on the prospects for Treasuries, pointed out that Greenspan had signalled there would not be the aggressive tightening seen in 1994.
"The Fed will just be tinkering at the edges, rather than making a major cyclical move," he said.
Chester said bond markets could withstand such slight moves, and in the longer term bonds would be a good buy.
Adrian Owens, European economist at Julius Baer Investments in London, said the widening in the T-note/Bund spread was a short term phenomenon, as the Fed could hike rates in March.
"Once people start to see more signals of growth in Europe, we'll start to see that spread reversing," he said.
He said European yields would rise as real activity picked up in Europe, even though the inflation threat was likely to remain subdued.

Owens said investors would be advised to shift positions to the short end of the yield curve to gain protection from any sell-off, while those investors who were unable to hold cash should look to move into dollar-bloc bonds after the first rate hike was over with.
But Wattret took a less optimistic view.

"I'm a bear of all the bond markets," said Wattret. "Treauries haven't full discounted a rate hike, and all the risks in Europe lie on one side -- that growth will pick up and by the end of the first quarter it will be clear there is no scope for rate cuts."
